report:
Based on my research, the evidence does **not** support the answer "yes." The strongest available evidence indicates that saw palmetto is **no more effective than placebo** for improving BPH symptoms in the longer term.

**Key evidence:**

- **NEJM 2006 (Bent et al.)**: A one-year, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT of 225 men with moderate-to-severe BPH found saw palmetto (160 mg twice daily) was *not superior to placebo* for improving urinary symptoms or objective measures such as prostate size or urinary flow rate. ([NEJM](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa053085))

- **STEP Trial (2011, Barry et al.)**: A 72-week multicenter RCT of 369 men used escalating doses of saw palmetto (up to 960 mg/day—three times the typical dose). Saw palmetto was *no more effective than placebo* for any primary or secondary outcome, including AUASI symptom scores, nocturia, or sexual function. ([Harvard Health Blog](https://www.health.harvard.edu/blog/saw-palmetto-fails-to-relieve-bph-symptoms-in-new-harvard-study-201109291923); [Gold Journal abstract](https://www.goldjournal.net/article/S0090-4295(11)01132-0/fulltext))

- **Cochrane Review (Tacklind et al.)**: The updated Cochrane systematic review concluded that *Serenoa repens* monotherapy provides "little to no benefits" for men with lower urinary tract symptoms due to benign prostatic enlargement. ([Cochrane](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001423_serenoa-repens-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia); [AAFP summary](https://www.aafp.org/afp/2024/0500/cochrane-saw-palmetto-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia))

- **NCCIH (NIH)****: The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health states that large trials have found saw palmetto no more effective than placebo for BPH symptoms. ([NCCIH](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/providers/digest/spotlight-on-saw-palmetto-science))

**Counterpoint:** Earlier, smaller trials and a 1998 JAMA meta-analysis suggested modest symptom improvements, but these studies suffered from methodological limitations (small sample sizes, short duration, inconsistent dosing). The larger, higher-quality, longer-term trials that followed failed to confirm these benefits.

**Conclusion:** The best long-term, placebo-controlled evidence—including two major RCTs and the Cochrane review—indicates that saw palmetto does **not** improve BPH symptoms beyond placebo in the longer term. The answer to your question should be **no**, not yes.
